# AI-Driven Personalized Recommendation Systems and Online Consumer Impulse Buying Behavior: A Systematic Literature Review and Bibliometric Network Analysis

**Author:** Le Phuc Hai (Lê Phúc Hải)  
**Affiliation:** NCSKIT.org (Independent Research Group)  
**ORCID:** [https://orcid.org/0009-0004-1215-5023](https://orcid.org/0009-0004-1215-5023)  
**Correspondence:** [hailp@ncskit.org](mailto:hailp@ncskit.org)

---

## HIGHLIGHTS
- Screens 2,500 Dimensions records (2018-2026) into a Broad Context Corpus (N = 1,152) and Core AI-Impulse Corpus (n = 84).
- Extracts 38 inductive terms (463 links, 5 clusters) from the Core Corpus alongside a 26-concept theory map.
- Separates cold-start fluency from cumulative e-satisfaction (P4a-P4b) and competing interactions (b3 > 0 vs. b3 < 0).
- Audits construct gaps: 0% multiplicative interaction and 1.19% reactance in Core AI-impulse abstracts.
- Links tiered ethical friction to binding EU DSA mandates, non-binding FTC guidance, and A/B trials.

---

## ABSTRACT
The rapid deployment of artificial intelligence (AI)-powered personalized recommendation systems across digital retailing platforms has shifted electronic commerce from deliberate keyword-driven search toward algorithmically curated discovery. Yet academic inquiry into the cognitive-affective mechanics governing AI-mediated impulsive consumption remains fragmented. Following PRISMA 2020 reporting principles and the TCCM framework, this study evaluates 2,500 initial records retrieved from the Dimensions scholarly database (exported November 28, 2026; 2018-2026 window; acknowledging Dimensions' 2,500-record export ceiling). Deterministic Title/Abstract screening yielded a **Broad Algorithmic & Digital Commerce Context Corpus** ($N = 1,152$ peer-reviewed journal articles) and, via strict co-occurrence of AI/recommendation and impulse-buying terms in Title/Abstract, a **Core AI-Impulse Corpus** ($n = 84$).

Inductive corpus-extracted co-word clustering ($DF \ge 5$, greedy modularity optimization, 38 terms, 463 links) on the Core Corpus identifies five empirical themes spanning impulse buying and personalized recommendations, AI/S-O-R framing, trust and purchase intention, algorithmic short-video/FOMO (TikTok Shop), and purchase decision drivers, supplemented by a 26-concept theory-driven map (Appendix B). Construct-separated lexical audits reveal zero explicit tests of cognitive-affective multiplicative interaction ($0.00\%$), zero curvilinear inverted-U tests ($0.00\%$ in Core; $1.48\%$ in Broad), and scarce reactance/manipulative-intent framing ($1.19\%$ in Core; $0.78\%$ in Broad). Advancing beyond static additive S-O-R models, we formulate a Dynamic Dual-Path S-O-R Framework separating in-session cognitive fluency (cold-start) from cumulative e-satisfaction (repeat sessions), specifying competing interaction hypotheses ($b_3 > 0$ synergistic permission vs. $b_3 < 0$ hot/cool override), and integrating endogenous surveillance reactance (P1), candidate self-regulatory strain (P7a/P7b), and a recursive post-purchase regret loop (P8).

**Keywords**: Artificial Intelligence; Personalized Recommendation Systems; Online Impulse Buying; Dual-Path S-O-R Model; PRISMA 2020; Bibliometrics; Cognitive Fit Theory; Ego Depletion; Algorithmic Dark Patterns.

---

## 1. INTRODUCTION

### 1.1. Background and The Algorithmic Retailing Paradigm Shift
In contemporary digital retailing ecosystems, consumers no longer navigate static, hierarchical category trees (Shanahan et al., 2019; Xiao & Benbasat, 2018). Instead, they are continuously enveloped within dynamic, hyper-personalized information streams driven by deep neural collaborative filtering, transformer-based sequential recommenders, and real-time behavioral telemetry (Al-Natour et al., 2011; Hallikainen et al., 2022). The foundational architecture of consumer discovery has shifted from deliberative, keyword-driven item retrieval (*search-based shopping*) to serendipitous, algorithmically triggered consumption (*discovery-based shopping*) (Sundar & Kim, 2019; Wang et al., 2022). Building on foundational digital retailing frameworks (Dwivedi et al., 2021; Guha et al., 2021), the proliferation of Large Language Model (LLM)-powered conversational shopping agents and Generative AI interfaces between 2023 and 2026 (Do Xuan Nguyen & Nguyen, 2026; Huang & Ahmad, 2026; Pang et al., 2026) enables platforms to anticipate and shape latent consumer desires in real time.

A primary behavioral outcome of this algorithmic immersion is online impulse buying (OIB) (defined as sudden, hedonically complex, and unplanned purchase decisions characterized by diminished deliberative cognitive evaluation) (Beatty & Ferrell, 1998; Rook & Fisher, 1995). Prior systematic reviews establish that unplanned purchasing constitutes a substantial share of digital commerce activity, catalyzed by algorithmic discovery feeds, flash recommendations, and frictionless one-click checkout infrastructures (Chan et al., 2017; Zheng et al., 2019). While practitioners celebrate predictive personalization as an engine of customer lifetime value and transaction velocity, consumer psychologists express growing scholarly concern regarding the ethical boundaries of algorithmic nudging, choice architecture manipulation, and the erosion of consumer self-regulatory willpower (Baumeister, 2002; Kumaran & Shobhana, 2026; Sweller, 1988).

### 1.2. Problem Statement, Salience Audit, and Positioning Relative to Prior Reviews
Despite substantial growth in empirical scholarship over the past decade, literature examining the nexus of AI recommendation systems and impulsive buying remains siloed across computer science, information systems (IS), and consumer psychology. A construct-separated lexical salience scan of Title and Abstract fields across our **Core AI-Impulse Corpus** ($n = 84$) and **Broad Context Corpus** ($N = 1,152$) indicates that while S-O-R framing appears in $20.24\%$ ($n = 17$) of Core abstracts ($13.89\%$, $n = 160$ in Broad), explicit mentions of psychological reactance or manipulative intent ($1.19\%$, $n = 1$ in Core; $0.78\%$, $n = 9$ in Broad), curvilinear or inverted-U thresholds ($0.00\%$ in Core; $1.48\%$, $n = 17$ in Broad), multiplicative cognitive-affective interactions ($0.00\%$ in both Core and Broad), ego depletion or cognitive load ($4.76\%$, $n = 4$ in Core; $1.48\%$, $n = 17$ in Broad), post-purchase regret or dissonance ($8.33\%$, $n = 7$ in Core; $4.25\%$, $n = 49$ in Broad), and Generative AI/LLM agents ($0.00\%$ in Core; $1.30\%$, $n = 15$ in Broad) remain scarce. Three core theoretical fault lines motivate our synthesis:

1. Theoretical Fragmentation of Algorithmic Stimuli (The S-O-R Disconnect):
   While the classical Stimulus-Organism-Response (S-O-R) paradigm (Mehrabian & Russell, 1974; Jacoby, 2002) provides an established environmental psychology foundation, early retail studies operationalized "Stimuli" primarily as static website atmospherics (e.g., color, layout, navigation structure; Eroglu et al., 2001). In algorithmic commerce, stimuli are dynamic, adaptive, and agentic. Crucially, literature exhibits sharp disagreement on whether algorithmic attributes, specifically *Perceived Personalization (PP)*, *Perceived Recommendation Accuracy (ACC)*, and *Recommendation Novelty & Serendipity (NOV)*, operate harmoniously or create conflicting psychological appraisals (Al-Natour et al., 2011; Ampadu et al., 2022; Gallin & Portes, 2024; Shanahan et al., 2019).

2. The Dual-Path Cognitive-Affective Divide (Organismic Processes):
   Existing literature often treats internal consumer organismic states as a monolithic construct. While some scholars emphasize cognitive evaluations like cumulative e-satisfaction (ESAT) (Oliver, 1980, 1993; Spreng et al., 1996), others argue that impulse buying is primarily an affective, visceral response driven by emotional arousal and hedonic flow (Beatty & Ferrell, 1998; Verhagen & van Dolen, 2011). Extant research has yet to fully reconcile how cumulative satisfaction interacts with immediate cold-start fluency and visceral urges, or when over-personalization induces perceived algorithmic surveillance and reactance (Komiak & Benbasat, 2006; Xiao & Benbasat, 2007, 2018).

3. The Intention-Behavior Gap and Self-Regulatory Boundaries:
   Traditional marketing models frequently conflate the psychological *urge to buy impulsively (UBI)* with the enacted *online impulse buying behavior (OIB)*. However, empirical consumer psychology demonstrates that an impulse urge does not inevitably result in transactional checkout (Badgaiyan & Verma, 2015; Rook & Fisher, 1995). Candidate self-regulatory mechanisms, including resource depletion (Baumeister, 2002; Baumeister et al., 2007; Vohs & Faber, 2007) alongside cognitive load theory (Sweller, 1988) and multilab replication debates (Hagger et al., 2016), require careful integration into dynamic models of algorithmic retailing.

To clarify incremental positioning, Table 1 contrasts this review against prior landmark reviews and temporal S-O-R models (Chan et al., 2017; Mariani et al., 2022; Redine et al., 2022; Tobon & Abril, 2024; Kumaran & Shobhana, 2026).

### 1.3. Research Objectives and Formal Research Questions
To resolve these theoretical fault lines, this study executes an integrative multi-method investigation combining the PRISMA 2020 systematic review protocol with VOSviewer science mapping and the TCCM synthesis framework. Specifically, we address three overarching research questions:
- **RQ1**: *What is the intellectual structure, thematic cluster architecture, and temporal evolution of international scholarship investigating AI recommendation systems and online impulse buying?*
- **RQ2**: *Through what dual-path cognitive-affective mechanisms do algorithmic stimuli influence consumer organismic states, and how do these states mediate the translation into impulsive purchasing urges and behaviors?*
- **RQ3**: *What psychological and technological boundary conditions govern this translation, and what future research agenda and ethical guardrails are necessary for sustainable algorithmic retailing?*

### 1.4. Paper Structure
The remainder of this paper is structured as follows. Section 2 delineates the systematic review methodology, detailing the PRISMA 2020 protocol, search strings, TCCM framing, text-mining gap audit protocol, and VOSviewer co-occurrence parameters. Section 3 presents the bibliometric performance analysis, VOSviewer quantitative cluster metrics and science mapping, and the TCCM empirical synthesis matrix. Section 4 articulates the integrative conceptual framework, develops eight core theoretical propositions (P1-P8, encompassing cold-start vs. cumulative paths P4a/P4b, affective mediation P5a, competing interaction P5b, and regulatory strain P7a/P7b), and outlines an empirical testing strategy. Section 5 discusses theoretical contributions, tiered ethical friction implications, details the 5-pillar future research agenda, acknowledges study limitations, and concludes.



## 2. METHODOLOGY: THE PRISMA 2020 PROTOCOL AND BIBLIOMETRIC DESIGN

### 2.1. Methodological Design and Agnostic Search Strategy
To prevent confirmation bias, the identification strategy adhered to an agnostic three-block Boolean structure covering technological stimuli (AI recommendation engines), behavioral outcomes (impulse purchasing), and digital retail contexts. Theoretical frameworks (such as S-O-R) and mediating constructs (such as e-satisfaction) were intentionally excluded from search strings so thematic clusters emerged inductively (Paul & Criado, 2020).

Searches were executed on November 28, 2026 in the Dimensions scholarly database (`full data` search scope, bibliographic export format), selected for its extensive coverage of interdisciplinary research across artificial intelligence, data science, and applied digital commerce. Large-scale bibliometric benchmarks by Thelwall (2018) and Visser et al. (2021) demonstrate that Dimensions achieves publication coverage comparable to, and in technology and applied computing domains often broader than, Scopus and Web of Science. Because Dimensions indexes diverse document types, rigorous programmatic filtering was applied to isolate peer-reviewed journal articles with valid Digital Object Identifiers (DOIs). The exact Boolean query executed in Dimensions (`full data`) is shown below:

```text
("artificial intelligence" OR "AI" OR "recommendation system*" OR "recommender system*" OR "algorithmic recommendation*" OR "personalized recommendation*" OR "deep learning recommendation*" OR "collaborative filtering")
AND
("impulse buying" OR "impulsive buying" OR "impulse purchase*" OR "spontaneous purchase*" OR "unplanned purchase*" OR "urge to buy impulsively")
AND
("e-commerce" OR "online shopping" OR "digital retailing" OR "electronic commerce" OR "social commerce" OR "mobile commerce")
```

To ensure disciplinary relevance and temporal precision at the database-retrieval stage, three native Dimensions interface filters were applied simultaneously:
- **Publication Type**: `Article`.
- **Fields of Research (ANZSRC 2020)**: `3506 Marketing` OR `35 Commerce, Management, Tourism and Services` OR `3503 Business Systems In Context` OR `3504 Commercial Services`.
- **Publication Year**: `2018` OR `2019` OR `2020` OR `2021` OR `2022` OR `2023` OR `2024` OR `2025` OR `2026`.

### 2.2. Eligibility Criteria and TCCM Framework Framing
The screening protocol was framed around the TCCM Framework (Theory, Context, Characteristics, Methodology), recognized as a widely adopted framework for systematic reviews in marketing and retailing (Paul & Rosado-Serrano, 2019; Paul & Criado, 2020):
- Theory (T): Studies examining behavioral, psychological, or information processing mechanisms (e.g., S-O-R, Cognitive Fit Theory, Dual-Process Theory, Self-Regulation).
- Context (C): Digital retailing environments including electronic commerce, mobile retailing, social commerce, and livestream shopping platforms.
- Characteristics (C): Algorithmic system attributes (personalization, accuracy, novelty, transparency) and consumer internal states (fluency, e-satisfaction, arousal, urge).
- Methodology (M): Rigorous empirical investigations (laboratory experiments, field surveys, neuro-marketing, structural equation modeling, fsQCA) alongside foundational conceptual and systematic review benchmarks that establish core construct taxonomies.

We established four explicit Inclusion Criteria (IC) and four Exclusion Criteria (EC):
- **IC1**: Published in peer-reviewed scholarly journals between January 2018 and November 2026 (excluding pre-2018, missing-year, and post-2026 records).
- **IC2**: Empirical investigation or foundational conceptual/review benchmark explicitly analyzing AI/algorithmic recommendation features alongside consumer impulse buying, unplanned/spontaneous purchasing, consumer habits, or customer decision-making dynamics.
- **IC3**: For empirical studies, clear reporting of sample size, analytical technique, and theoretical grounding (foundational conceptual/review benchmarks retained under IC2 are exempted from sample-size reporting).
- **IC4**: Indexed in Dimensions carrying a valid DOI.
- **EC1**: Non-journal or non-eligible Dimensions records, including conference proceedings, book chapters/series, preprints, and retracted notices.
- **EC2**: Missing abstracts, purely algorithmic optimization studies, or off-topic records lacking an explicit impulse-buying, consumer-habit, or purchasing-behavior nexus alongside consumer/commerce context in Title/Abstract.
- **EC3**: Clinical/medical domains unrelated to consumer behavior.
- **EC4**: Duplicate DOI or title records within the Dimensions export.

### 2.3. The 4-Stage Two-Tier Screening Funnel (2,500 to 1,152 Broad / 84 Core Articles)
Adhering to the PRISMA 2020 statement (Page et al., 2021), the data collection and screening process progressed through four transparent, auditable stages implemented via deterministic Python rule-based Title/Abstract filtering (`run_full_slr_from_dimensions.py`):
1. Identification: Database retrieval from Dimensions (`full data` scope) on November 28, 2026 yielded 2,500 initial records with valid DOIs (`0` duplicate DOIs detected under EC4). Because Dimensions CSV exports are capped at 2,500 records per export, this initial pool represents a bounded top-2,500 sample rather than an uncapped census.
2. Pre-Screen Filtering (Window, Venue & Quality): Programmatic filtering against IC1 and EC1-EC2 confirmed 0 out-of-window records (within 2018-2026), and removed 45 conference/book-series/preprint records, 7 records lacking abstracts, and 2 retracted notices (`n = 54` total pre-screen exclusions), leaving 2,446 eligible peer-reviewed journal articles.
3. Title & Abstract Screening and Sensitivity Breakdown: Because Dimensions searched `full data` (including full-text and cited-reference metadata), deterministic lexical screening against EC2 and EC3 excluded 310 clinical/medical non-consumer studies and 984 off-topic records lacking an explicit impulse-buying, consumer-habit, or purchasing-behavior nexus alongside commerce context in Title/Abstract (`n = 1,294` T/A exclusions), yielding the **Broad Algorithmic & Digital Commerce Context Corpus** ($N = 1,152$). A Title/Abstract sensitivity audit across these 1,152 records revealed that 309 contain strict AI/recommendation terms in Title/Abstract, 386 contain explicit impulse-buying terms in Title/Abstract, and **84 records contain both AI/recommendation and impulse-buying terms in Title/Abstract**, forming our **Core AI-Impulse Corpus** ($n = 84$). Only 15 records ($1.30\%$) across the 1,152 corpus mention Generative AI or LLM terms in Title/Abstract.
4. Verification Scope & Co-Occurrence Parameters: Manual Title/Abstract verification was conducted on the 84-article Core AI-Impulse Corpus and the Table 6 empirical synthesis studies; automated Python screening governed the remaining Broad Context Corpus without full-text two-coder verification (acknowledged in Section 5.4). On the 84-article Core Corpus, inductive corpus-extracted 2- and 3-gram co-occurrence mapping ($DF \ge 5$, greedy modularity clustering, 38 terms, 463 links) was computed and exported in VOSviewer-compatible `.txt` format (`vosviewer_core_map.txt`, `vosviewer_core_network.txt`), supplemented by a 26-concept theory-driven concept map in Appendix B.

## 3. BIBLIOMETRIC AND THEMATIC RESULTS

### 3.1. Performance Analysis: Publication Trajectories and Leading Outlets
Bibliometric performance analysis across our Broad Context Corpus ($N = 1,152$, 2018-2026) and nested Core AI-Impulse Corpus ($n = 84$) reveals a steep unnormalized growth trajectory across three phases, illustrated in Figure 2 (note: absolute counts are not normalized against overall Dimensions database expansion):
- Foundational Phase (2018–2020): Exploratory output totaling 53 Broad studies (4.6%; 5 Core studies), focusing on collaborative filtering, mobile commerce S-O-R cues, and early social commerce (Akram et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2019; Chopdar & Balakrishnan, 2020; Hu et al., 2019; Xiao & Benbasat, 2018).
- Expansion Phase (2021–2023): Acceleration totaling 233 Broad studies (20.2%; 18 Core studies), catalyzed by livestreaming cues, virtual streamers, and personalized product quality (Ampadu et al., 2022; Gao et al., 2023; Redine et al., 2022; Wu et al., 2021; Yin & Qiu, 2021).
- High-Velocity Algorithmic & Social Commerce Expansion (2024–2026): Output totaling 866 Broad studies (75.2%; 61 Core studies through November 2026), driven by short-video platforms, TikTok Shop, livestreaming curation, and early algorithmic dark-pattern investigations (Do Xuan Nguyen & Nguyen, 2026; Shamim & Misra, 2025; Truong et al., 2026). Only 15 studies (1.30%) in the Broad corpus explicitly mention Generative AI or LLM terms in Title/Abstract, indicating that empirical GenAI-impulse research remains nascent.

Table 2 presents the quantitative publication trajectory across the 1152 included studies, Table 3 ranks the Top 10 core dissemination outlets, and Figure 3 maps the geographic distribution across 84 contributing countries, confirming *Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services* ($n = 62$) and *Journal of Theoretical and Applied Electronic Commerce Research* ($n = 54$) as the leading academic venues.

### 3.2. Inductive Science Mapping of the Core AI-Impulse Corpus (n = 84)
To avoid circular confirmation of pre-selected theoretical categories, we performed **inductive corpus-extracted co-word network analysis** directly on the Titles and Abstracts of the Core AI-Impulse Corpus ($n = 84$). After removing publisher abstract boilerplate (e.g., *design methodology approach*, *practical implications*, *originality value*) and normalizing British/American spelling variants, 38 corpus-derived 2- and 3-gram terms met the minimum document-frequency threshold ($DF \ge 5$), forming 463 co-occurrence links. Greedy modularity optimization partitioned these 38 empirical terms into five distinct clusters (Table 5 and Figure 4), exported in VOSviewer-compatible tab-delimited format (`vosviewer_core_map.txt`, `vosviewer_core_network.txt`). Note that Figure 4 was rendered programmatically from this modularity solution rather than via the VOSviewer desktop GUI, and the pre-specified 26-concept theoretical dictionary is reported separately in Appendix B as a *Theory-Driven Concept Map*.

Detailed thematic synthesis of the five inductively detected clusters reveals the empirical structure of the Core AI-Impulse Corpus:

1. **Cluster 1 (Red): Impulse Buying &amp; Personalized Outcomes** ($n = 17$ terms, 301 occurrences, $\text{APY} = 2024.76$). Anchored by `impulse buying`, `consumer buying behavior`, `consumer behavior`, `impulse purchase`, and `personalized recommendation`, this largest cluster captures core empirical tests linking personalized product feeds to unplanned purchasing (Ampadu et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2019; Do Xuan Nguyen &amp; Nguyen, 2026; Fadilah et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2025; Pal, 2025; Sholihah et al., 2025).
2. **Cluster 2 (Green): AI Systems &amp; S-O-R Framing** ($n = 8$ terms, 86 occurrences, $\text{APY} = 2025.21$). Anchored by `artificial intelligence`, `ai recommendation`, `s-o-r framework`, `recommendation system`, and `digital commerce`, this cluster demonstrates that S-O-R remains the dominant theoretical bridge connecting algorithmic stimuli to consumer responses (Amin, 2025; Cui et al., 2022; Li et al., 2025; Shamim &amp; Misra, 2025; Shi et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023).
3. **Cluster 3 (Blue): Trust, Intention &amp; Marketing Strategy** ($n = 6$ terms, 49 occurrences, $\text{APY} = 2025.04$). Anchored by `purchase intention`, `marketing strategies`, `trust`, `marketing practices`, and `brand loyalty`, this cluster reflects managerial and cognitive-trust evaluations of virtual recommendation agents and AI-enabled retail interfaces (Gao &amp; Liang, 2025; Jain &amp; Gandhi, 2021; Liu et al., 2020; Mukit et al., 2021; Saad &amp; Choura, 2022).
4. **Cluster 4 (Amber): Short-Video Algorithms, FOMO &amp; TikTok Shop** ($n = 5$ terms, 29 occurrences, $\text{APY} = 2025.69$). Anchored by `recommendation algorithm`, `fear of missing out (fomo)`, and `tiktok shop`, this recent sub-cluster captures short-video algorithmic feeds, social media silk-road dynamics, and manipulative or biased recommendation effects (Abbott et al., 2023; Ciocodeică et al., 2025; Liang et al., 2025; Ooi et al., 2025; Truong et al., 2026).
5. **Cluster 5 (Violet): Purchase Decision Drivers** ($n = 2$ terms, 14 occurrences, $\text{APY} = 2025.07$). Anchored by `purchase decisions` and `influencing consumer`, representing general decision-making and urge-to-action framing within Core abstracts (Anoop &amp; Rahman, 2024; Wang et al., 2024).

## 4. CONCEPTUAL FRAMEWORK AND THEORETICAL PROPOSITIONS

### 4.1. From Generation 1.0 Filtering to Generation 2.0 Generative AI: Dynamic S-O-R Architecture
Synthesizing our bibliometric findings and the TCCM empirical matrix, we formulate an integrative Dynamic Dual-Path S-O-R Framework, illustrated in Figure 5. Crucially, to resolve the "AI-specificity disconnect" in prior retail literature, we explicitly distinguish between Algorithmic Generation 1.0 (predictive collaborative filtering and static item feeds, 2011-2021) and Algorithmic Generation 2.0 (Large Language Model conversational assistants, multimodal livestreaming cues, and real-time adaptive agents, 2023-2026). Whereas Generation 1.0 systems passively optimize item matching, Generation 2.0 systems inject social agency, conversational anthropomorphism, and micro-latency persuasion directly into the shopping journey (Huang & Ahmad, 2026; Ma et al., 2026; Pang et al., 2026). As summarized in Table 7, this shift substantially compresses deliberative cognitive latency and heightens cognitive load.

<td style="padding: 8px 12px;">Static visual carousels and passive behavioral filtering</td>
<td style="padding: 8px 12px;">Dynamic dialogue, real-time contextual persuasion, multimodal cues</td>
</tr>
<tr style="border-bottom: 1px solid #f1f5f9; background: #fdfdfd;">
<td style="padding: 8px 12px;"><strong>Perceived Agency &amp; Presence</strong></td>
<td style="padding: 8px 12px;">Low; perceived as a passive sorting utility</td>
<td style="padding: 8px 12px;">High; anthropomorphic social presence and parasocial intimacy</td>
</tr>
<tr style="border-bottom: 1px solid #f1f5f9;">
<td style="padding: 8px 12px;"><strong>Cognitive Appraisal Mechanism</strong></td>
<td style="padding: 8px 12px;">Cumulative cross-session e-satisfaction</td>
<td style="padding: 8px 12px;">In-session cognitive fluency and cold-start instant gratification</td>
</tr>
<tr style="border-bottom: 1px solid #f1f5f9; background: #fdfdfd;">
<td style="padding: 8px 12px;"><strong>Self-Regulatory Risk</strong></td>
<td style="padding: 8px 12px;">Filter bubble fatigue and moderate privacy concerns</td>
<td style="padding: 8px 12px;">Accelerated ego depletion and overt surveillance reactance</td>
</tr>

</table>

### 4.2. Resolving the Cold-Start Paradox and Endogenous Inverted-U Reactance (P1, P2)
A persistent temporal paradox in prior e-commerce literature is the reliance on cumulative e-satisfaction (which requires repeated cross-session transactions) to explain impulsive purchases on algorithmic discovery feeds such as TikTok Shop and Temu, where consumers frequently buy during cold-start first encounters. To reconcile this discrepancy, our framework integrates In-Session Cognitive Fluency (immediate processing ease and instant interface satisfaction) alongside cumulative cross-session e-satisfaction (ESAT) (Gallin & Portes, 2024; Shanahan et al., 2019; Srinivasan et al., 2002). According to Cognitive Fit Theory (Vessey, 1991), when an AI agent delivers information aligned with a consumer's mental schema during an active session, mental search friction drops immediately, generating instant cognitive fluency even without prior platform loyalty.

However, rather than assuming a monotonically linear positive effect, we model Perceived Personalization (PP) through an endogenous inverted-U (curvilinear) relationship. Grounded in foundational personalization-privacy paradox research (Awad & Krishnan, 2006; Aguirre et al., 2015) and algorithm appreciation vs. aversion studies (Logg et al., 2019), moderate personalization fosters cognitive fluency and e-satisfaction (Xiao & Benbasat, 2007). Conversely, when algorithmic targeting crosses an intrusive privacy threshold or employs deceptive dark patterns (Mathur et al., 2019), it endogenously triggers Algorithmic Surveillance Reactance within the same consumer (Brehm, 1966; Kumaran & Shobhana, 2026; Lau et al., 2026). Rather than acting purely as an external moderator, surveillance reactance emerges internally from excessive personalization, eroding trust and re-activating deliberative skepticism. Simultaneously, Perceived Recommendation Accuracy (ACC) drives expectancy confirmation (Al-Natour et al., 2011; Oliver, 1980). Therefore, we propose:
- **Proposition 1 (P1 - Curvilinear Personalization & Endogenous Surveillance Reactance):** *Perceived personalization exhibits an inverted-U relationship with in-session cognitive fluency and cumulative e-satisfaction, mediated in its downward tail by measurable surveillance reactance once algorithmic specificity crosses privacy, user-control, and transparency thresholds.*
- **Proposition 2 (P2):** *Perceived recommendation accuracy positively influences cognitive fluency and e-satisfaction through expectancy confirmation.*

### 4.3. Recommendation Novelty and the Affective Pathway (P3)
While accuracy confirms expectations, accuracy alone can result in monotonous, predictable suggestions that fail to generate impulsive excitement. Recommendation Novelty & Serendipity (NOV) (defined as the algorithmic presentation of unexpected yet notably attractive and relevant items; Feng et al., 2024; Lin, 2026) introduces hedonic surprise into the shopping journey. According to Environmental Psychology (Mehrabian & Russell, 1974), unexpected positive environmental stimuli provoke an immediate surge in physiological and emotional arousal. When consumers discover appealing items they did not intentionally search for, hedonic curiosity and pleasure are ignited, producing an immediate affective elevation (Lin, 2026). Therefore, we propose:
- **Proposition 3 (P3):** *Recommendation novelty and serendipity positively influence consumer emotional arousal and positive affect.*

### 4.4. Organismic States as the Dual Mediating and Multiplicative Bridge (P4a, P4b, P5, P5a, P5b)
In environmental psychology, internal organism states mediate the translation of ambient stimuli into behavioral urges. Traditional consumer decision models position impulse buying as an irrational departure from deliberate calculation (Rook & Fisher, 1995). Through our dual-path lens:

1. The Cognitive Bridge (Cumulative E-Satisfaction): Cumulative e-satisfaction produces a psychological state of affective comfort and disarmed vigilance. When a shopper experiences heightened satisfaction with the algorithmic interface, perceived transaction risk diminishes, cognitive defense mechanisms soften, and trust strengthens (Gallin & Portes, 2024; Oliver, 1993; Spreng et al., 1996). This psychological ease creates an open, receptive mindset that amplifies the spontaneous urge to buy impulsively.
2. The Affective Bridge (Emotional Arousal): Simultaneously, heightened emotional arousal directly stimulates visceral desire. Consumers experiencing hedonic excitement and flow states focus intensely on immediate gratification, diminishing attention to future budgetary constraints (Beatty & Ferrell, 1998; Verhagen & van Dolen, 2011).

Thus, in repeat-session engagements, cumulative cognitive evaluations and emotional arousal do not merely add together linearly; they interact according to the structural equation $UBI = b_1 \text{Cumulative ESAT} + b_2 \text{Arousal} + b_3 (\text{Cumulative ESAT} \times \text{Arousal})$, whereas first-encounter cold-start sessions operate primarily via In-Session Cognitive Fluency ($P_{4a}$). Under the synergistic permission hypothesis ($b_3 > 0$), emotional arousal without cognitive comfort leaves consumers hesitant due to perceived transaction risk, whereas cognitive satisfaction without affective arousal yields deliberate loyalty rather than spontaneous impulse buying (Do Xuan Nguyen & Nguyen, 2026). Conversely, to maximize empirical falsifiability, we specify a competing hot/cool override hypothesis ($b_3 < 0$) grounded in dual-system self-regulation theory (Metcalfe & Mischel, 1999; Hoch & Loewenstein, 1991), whereby extreme visceral ("hot") arousal overwhelms deliberative ("cool") cognitive evaluation even when cognitive satisfaction is low. To resolve the cold-start paradox cleanly, we separate immediate fluency from cumulative e-satisfaction in the propositions below:
- **Proposition 4a (P4a - Cold-Start Fluency):** *In-session cognitive fluency positively drives immediate UBI during first-encounter algorithmic browsing without requiring prior platform loyalty.*
- **Proposition 4b (P4b - Cumulative E-Satisfaction):** *Cumulative e-satisfaction mediates repeat-session algorithmic stimuli (personalization and accuracy) on UBI by lowering perceived relational risk.*
- **Proposition 5 (P5):** *Emotional arousal positively influences the urge to buy impulsively by amplifying visceral hedonic desire.*
- **Proposition 5a (P5a - Affective Mediation):** *Emotional arousal mediates the positive relationship between recommendation novelty/serendipity and the urge to buy impulsively.*
- **Proposition 5b (P5b - Competing Interaction Hypotheses):** *Cumulative e-satisfaction and emotional arousal interact to shape UBI ($b_3$ in the equation above), with the synergistic permission view predicting positive amplification ($b_3 > 0$) and the competing hot/cool override view predicting affective dominance ($b_3 < 0$).*

### 4.5. The Urge-to-Behavior Transition (P6)
The urge to buy impulsively (UBI) represents an acute, felt state of spontaneous desire that precedes transactional execution (Beatty & Ferrell, 1998; Rook & Fisher, 1995). In digital retail environments characterized by frictionless checkout architectures (e.g., Apple Pay, 1-click ordering, saved biometric credentials), the temporal latency between experiencing an impulse and executing payment is compressed to seconds. Extant empirical literature consistently validates that felt impulsive urges represent the most proximate psychological determinant of actual impulse buying behavior (Badgaiyan & Verma, 2015; Zheng et al., 2019). We therefore advance:
- **Proposition 6 (P6):** *The urge to buy impulsively positively influences online impulse buying behavior.*

### 4.6. Ego Depletion Boundary Condition (P7a, P7b) and Negative Recursive Feedback Loop (P8)
A persistent limitation of static S-O-R models is treating impulsive checkout as a terminal endpoint rather than an ongoing cyclic process. First, grounded in Baumeister's (2002) Strength Model of Self-Control, Vohs and Faber's (2007) experimental demonstration that self-regulatory depletion elevates impulsive spending urges, and Sweller's (1988) Cognitive Load Theory, sustained cognitive exertion can strain executive restraint (Baumeister et al., 2007; Kulal et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026). Because large-scale multilab replications report mixed effect sizes for classic depletion tasks (Hagger et al., 2016), we treat self-regulatory strain as a candidate mechanism tested alongside cognitive-load and opportunity-cost controls, acting both as an antecedent to felt urges and as a moderator of checkout execution:
- **Proposition 7a (P7a - Urge Elevation):** *Situational self-regulatory strain (ego depletion / cognitive load) positively elevates baseline urge to buy impulsively during high-velocity AI browsing.*
- **Proposition 7b (P7b - Checkout Amplification):** *Self-regulatory strain positively moderates the UBI-to-OIB transition, such that impulsive urges convert more readily into unplanned checkout under elevated cognitive fatigue.*

Second, we introduce a Negative Recursive Feedback Loop (P8) connecting short-term conversion to long-term platform equity. When platforms exploit ego depletion to trigger unbudgeted purchases, consumers frequently experience post-purchase regret and cognitive dissonance once self-regulatory clarity returns. This negative emotional aftermath erodes cumulative e-satisfaction in subsequent shopping sessions and primes heightened vigilance against future algorithmic surveillance (Kumaran & Shobhana, 2026). Thus:
- **Proposition 8 (P8 - Recursive Feedback Loop):** *Online impulse buying executed under high ego depletion induces post-purchase regret, which negatively feeds back to erode future cumulative e-satisfaction and amplify algorithmic surveillance reactance.*

### 4.7. Empirical Operationalization and Model Testing Strategy
To translate this theoretical architecture into falsifiable empirical tests without risking model over-parameterization, future quantitative investigations should adopt a two-tier methodological estimation strategy, summarized in Table 8:
1. Latent Quadratic and Multiplicative Structural Estimation (Testing P1 and P5b): Within cross-sectional or experimental designs, researchers should employ Latent Moderated Structural Equations (LMS) or Two-Stage PLS-SEM incorporating explicit quadratic terms ($PP^2$) to test the inverted-U personalization-reactance curve ($P_1$) alongside a multiplicative product indicator ($ESAT \times Arousal$) to validate the permission-kinetic energy interaction ($P_{5b}$), supplemented by Johnson-Neyman floodlight analysis to identify exact ego depletion thresholds ($P_{7a}, P_{7b}$).
2. Cross-Lagged Panel Modeling (Testing P8): To empirically capture the negative recursive feedback loop ($P_8$) across sequential shopping episodes without violating cross-sectional causality assumptions, researchers should implement a three-wave Random-Intercept Cross-Lagged Panel Model (RI-CLPM) linking Time $t$ depletion-induced impulse purchases and post-purchase regret to Time $t+1$ cumulative e-satisfaction and leftward shifts in privacy tolerance thresholds.

**Table 8: Conceptual Proposition Status and Recommended Empirical Testing Strategy**

| Proposition | Hypothesized Mechanism / Path | Conceptual & Literature Status | Recommended Testing Strategy |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **P1** | Inverted-U Personalization $\rightarrow$ Measurable Surveillance Reactance | Under-tested in impulse buying (requires nonlinear validation) | LMS / Two-Stage PLS-SEM / RSA ($PP^2$) + Surveillance Reactance mediation |
| **P2 & P3** | Accuracy $\rightarrow$ Fluency/ESAT; Novelty $\rightarrow$ Arousal | Established baseline in prior SEM/experimental studies | PLS-SEM / Multi-Group Moderation |
| **P4a & P4b** | Cold-Start In-Session Fluency vs. Repeat Cumulative ESAT | Conceptual distinction proposed to resolve cold-start paradox | Multi-group (New vs. Repeat Shoppers) |
| **P5 & P5a** | Emotional Arousal & Affective Mediation $\rightarrow$ UBI | Established baseline in environmental psychology | Bootstrapped Indirect Effects |
| **P5b** | Competing Interaction: Synergistic ($b_3 > 0$) vs. Hot/Cool Override ($b_3 < 0$) | Unresolved competing hypotheses | Latent Moderated Structural Equations (LMS) |
| **P6** | UBI $\rightarrow$ Online Impulse Buying (OIB) | Well-established behavioral link in impulse literature | Behavioral checkout telemetry / Survey |
| **P7a & P7b** | Candidate Self-Control Strain (Urge Elevation & Checkout Amplification) | Mixed replication evidence (Hagger et al., 2016) | Dual-task cognitive load (P7a) + Johnson-Neyman moderation (P7b) |
| **P8** | Depletion-Induced OIB $\rightarrow$ Regret $\rightarrow$ Future ESAT & Reactance | Nascent longitudinal feedback mechanism | 3-wave RI-CLPM, Experience Sampling (ESM) & Platform Return Logs |

## 5. DISCUSSION, FUTURE RESEARCH AGENDA, AND MANAGERIAL IMPLICATIONS

### 5.1. Theoretical Paradigm Shift: From Static Conversion to Dynamic Algorithmic Well-being
Rather than viewing algorithmic retailing through an isolated, static conversion lens, this review repositions consumer impulse buying research from a Static Conversion Optimization Paradigm toward a Dynamic Algorithmic Well-being Paradigm. Our conceptual synthesis makes three integrated advances. First, by contrasting Generation 1.0 collaborative filtering with Generation 2.0 conversational Generative AI (Table 7), we specify how anthropomorphic social agency and micro-latency persuasion compress deliberative evaluation while accelerating cognitive fatigue (Huang & Ahmad, 2026; Pang et al., 2026). Second, we propose that in-session cognitive fluency (P4a) and cumulative e-satisfaction (P4b) operate through separable temporal mechanisms and interact with emotional arousal under competing hypotheses ($b_3 > 0$ synergistic permission vs. $b_3 < 0$ hot/cool override, P5b) (Do Xuan Nguyen & Nguyen, 2026; Hoch & Loewenstein, 1991; Metcalfe & Mischel, 1999). Third, by merging surveillance reactance into an endogenous inverted-U personalization curve ($P_1$), elevating reactance and post-purchase regret to measurable nodes, and framing self-regulatory strain ($P_{7a}, P_{7b}$) alongside cognitive-load and replication debates (Hagger et al., 2016; Sweller, 1988; Vohs & Faber, 2007), we outline how short-term conversion tactics may erode long-term customer trust.

### 5.2. Managerial and Ethical Implications: Tiered "Ethical Friction" for Sustainable CLV
For retail executives and algorithm architects, our dynamic model elevates ethical design from mere legal compliance to a core Customer Lifetime Value (CLV) retention strategy:
- Calibrating the March (1991) Exploitation-Exploration Ratio: Drawing on James March's (1991) organizational learning paradigm, platforms must balance *exploitation* (high-accuracy matching) with *exploration* (serendipitous discovery) to stimulate curiosity without crossing the inverted-U surveillance threshold (Li et al., 2025).
- Tiered "Ethical Friction" Architecture and Regulatory Alignment: Rather than applying blanket checkout delays that harm user experience, platforms should evaluate tiered ethical friction calibrated by product regret risk, aligning interface design with binding statutory mandates under the European Union Digital Services Act (DSA) (Regulation (EU) 2022/2065, Article 25 prohibiting deceptive dark patterns; European Parliament and Council, 2022) and non-binding regulatory guidance in the U.S. Federal Trade Commission (FTC) Staff Report on digital dark patterns (Federal Trade Commission, 2022; Mathur et al., 2019). For *low-regret, low-ticket consumables*, frictionless checkout preserves convenience. Conversely, for *high-regret, high-involvement discretionary items* encountered during late-night sessions or rapid browsing streaks indicative of cognitive strain, platforms should test smart cooling-off nudges, transparent recommendation rationales ("*Why am I seeing this?*"), and optional 24-hour cart locks (Tobon & Abril, 2024). Crucially, these interventions must be validated through randomized A/B field trials that jointly measure short-term conversion, post-purchase return rates, and long-term Customer Lifetime Value (CLV) before platform-wide rollout.

### 5.3. An Actionable 5-Pillar Future Research Agenda
To guide scholarship over the coming decade, we articulate a structured 5-Pillar Future Research Agenda, accompanied by explicit empirical research questions in Table 9:

1. **Pillar 1: Methodological Triangulation (fsQCA and Necessary Condition Analysis - NCA)**: Extant scholarship relies heavily on linear, symmetrical regression techniques (CB-SEM, PLS-SEM). Future research must embrace causal complexity through fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA) and NCA to identify asymmetric configurations of algorithmic stimuli that are necessary or sufficient for high impulse conversion.
2. **Pillar 2: Experimental Ego Depletion and Real-Time Cognitive Load Manipulation**: Rather than relying on self-reported trait self-control scales, experimental consumer researchers should deploy dual-task laboratory manipulations (e.g., Stroop color-word interference, cognitive load memory burdens) to causally test the depletion boundary condition under varying algorithmic interface speeds.
3. **Pillar 3: Neuromarketing and Physiological Telemetry**: Integrate multi-modal neuro-physiological measurements, such as eye-tracking gaze fixation, pupillometry (arousal index), galvanic skin response (GSR), and facial expression analysis, to capture non-conscious affective arousal during live recommendation scrolling.
4. **Pillar 4: Ethical Algorithmic Guardrails, Dark Patterns, and Consumer Cooling-Off Mechanics**: Investigate how platform-enforced ethical guardrails (e.g., algorithmic nutrition labels, voluntary spending friction) impact consumer trust, perceived paternalism, and long-term customer lifetime value versus short-term impulse revenue.
5. **Pillar 5: Generative AI, Conversational Agents, and Cross-Cultural Longitudinal Designs**: Examine how conversational LLM shopping agents substantially alter social presence and anthropomorphic trust (Huang & Ahmad, 2026; Ma et al., 2026). Furthermore, deploy longitudinal latent growth curve modeling across Western and Eastern e-commerce platforms to capture temporal changes in algorithmic tolerance.

### 5.4. Limitations and Conclusion
In accordance with the PRISMA 2020 reporting standard (Item 23c; Page et al., 2021), several methodological boundaries of this review warrant transparent acknowledgment. First, this review relies on a single-source export from Dimensions, whose standard CSV export is capped at 2,500 records per query; consequently, the retrieved dataset represents a bounded top-2,500 sample rather than an uncapped census across Dimensions, Scopus, and Web of Science. Second, because Dimensions' `full data` search matched full-text and cited-reference metadata, only 84 of the 1,152 Broad Context articles contain both strict AI/recommendation and impulse-buying terms in Title/Abstract; our two-tier reporting isolates these 84 Core studies for inductive mapping and empirical synthesis while retaining the remaining records as digital-commerce context. Third, automated deterministic Title/Abstract screening governed the 1,152 Broad corpus without full-text dual-coder verification (manual verification was focused on the 84 Core studies and Table 6), and annual growth counts are unnormalized for overall Dimensions database expansion. Fourth, excluding non-journal outlets (EC1) omits computer science conferences (e.g., ACM RecSys, KDD, CHI), while Dimensions' predominantly English-language metadata may underrepresent regional non-English studies. Finally, because underlying empirical studies rely heavily on cross-sectional surveys, causal claims regarding temporal feedback dynamics ($P_8$) require longitudinal panel validation.

Notwithstanding these limitations, this study advances international retailing scholarship by integrating two-tier PRISMA 2020 screening (Core $n = 84$; Broad $N = 1,152$), inductive corpus-extracted co-word mapping across five modularity clusters, construct-separated lexical gap audits, and a Dynamic Dual-Path S-O-R Framework for sustainable digital commerce.


### Data Availability Statement
The complete PRISMA 2020 screening ledger (`paper1a_osf_screening_log.csv`, documenting all 2,500 records exported from Dimensions on November 28, 2026 alongside exact tier/exclusion codes yielding $N = 1,152$ Broad and $n = 84$ Core journal articles), the clean datasets (`dimensions_clean_included.csv`, `dimensions_core_ai_impulse.csv`), VOSviewer-compatible network exports (`vosviewer_core_map.txt`, `vosviewer_core_network.txt`), and Python audit scripts (`run_full_slr_from_dimensions.py`) are prepared for Open Science Framework (OSF) archiving. Because Dimensions continuously updates its live index and caps single exports at 2,500 records, exact reproducibility relies on the archived DOI ledger and the raw export file (`Dimensions-Publication-2026-11-28_08-40-19.csv`, SHA-256: `508f0b3af60b1d339d8a570ea71a9665894c49c19fb058bfd52f0b51cb84493a`), governed by Digital Science licensing.
